newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan banks cutting less profitable loan assets.
newsitem.headline: Japan banks cutting less profitable loan assets.

text.p: Japan's big banks have actively cut less profitable loan assets with the aim of improving their capital adequacy ratios and increasing the profitability of their assets, analysts and industry sources said on Wednesday.
The three long-term credit banks have been particularly active, they said.
An official at the Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan Ltd (LTCB) said it cut its loan assets by about 500 billion yen in the six months to September 30, the first half of 1996/97.
An official at Nippon Credit Bank Ltd (NCB) said it has been steadily reducing its loan assets to improve its capital adequacy ratio.

Yoshinobu Yamada, an analyst at Merrill Lynch Japan, said: "Cutting less profitable loans is a sign that Japanese bankers' way of thinking about lending is finally changing. They are becoming more serious about improving profitability."
Big Japanese banks, facing fierce competition in local markets, have tended in the past to concentrate on building up large loan assets, rather than on the profitability of such assets.

While the LTCB plans to cut less profitable loans by one trillion yen by next March 31 under a restructuring programme, other major banks are also trying to reduce the amount of such loans, Yamada added.

For instance, the business daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun reported on Wednesday that the amount of loan credits liquidated by 10 commercial banks and the three long-term credit banks -- LTCB, NCB and the Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd (IBJ) -- was estimated at around two trillion yen at the end of September, up 300 billion yen from six months earlier.

These are "performing" loans to large, financially healthy companies, and thus the loan spread -- the difference between the cost of obtaining funds and returns from lending -- is thin, analysts and the sources said.
But buyers such as foreign banks, regional banks and life insurance companies are often able to enjoy better returns than by investing in money markets, they said.
Liquidation of such loan assets helped big banks achieve the minimum eight percent capital adequacy ratio at the end of September. The ratio was set by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS).
Japan's 20 biggest banks each said this week that their capital adequacy ratios at the end of September were above eight percent.

But among the 20 banks, the capital adequacy ratios of the Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd (IBJ), NCB, Sakura Bank Ltd, Fuji Bank Ltd and Daiwa Bank Ltd were still below the desirable level of nine percent.
The yen's decline against the dollar was one reason why the capital adequacy ratio of the IBJ fell from 8.59 percent at the end of March to about 8.4 percent, an IBJ official said.

Many of the big Japanese banks posted losses in 1995/96, ended March 31, after aggressively disposing of non-performing loans last financial year, which resulted in a decline in the ratio of banks' capital to their risk-weighted assets.
Analysts said Japanese banks intend to boost their capital adequacy ratios to 10 percent in order to better compete with their Western rivals in international markets.
